pi.name: Gaia Stucky de Quay
bio: Hi, I'm Gaia (she/her). I'm an Assistant Professor at the Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences (EAPS) at MIT. Born in Brazil, with Spanish citizenship, and raised in Portugal, I feel right at home in the warm, tropical climate of Boston. Before I ended up here, I obtained my PhD from Imperial College London (with a UChicago internship), and an MSci from University College London where I first fell in love with Earth and Planetary Sciences. Following that, I completed postdocs at UT Austin and my Assistant Professorship at MIT in 2023 and I am looking forward to getting my new group and lab up and running. In general, I'm interested in why landscapes look the way they do. I've looked at channels buried below the seabed, canyons in Iceland, and lakes on Mars -- but I'm always looking for new places to explore! My weak spot is a waterfall, how can you not love them? Outside of work, I love tennis, triathlons, art, reading, and so many other things that I can't fit here. Check out the amazing members of our group below :)

members.name: Abdallah Zaki
members.bio: I’m Abdallah (he/him). I was born in Egypt, earned my PhD at the University of Geneva in Switzerland, and did postdoctoral work at Caltech and the University of Texas at Austin. My research asks three questions: (1) How do water-formed landscapes record climate, tectonics, and crustal structure on planetary surfaces? (2) When, where, and for how long did water flow on Mars? (3) How can we read these processes from the geomorphic and sedimentary record at outcrop, basin, and planetary scales? I use a blend of tools, including remote sensing, field observations, laboratory analyses, geochronology, and climate modeling, to reconstruct ancient environments and landscapes, and to assess their habitability. When I’m not reading the history of planets, I’m reading the history of us: who we are and how we got here. I chase the same story in music and in the streets of every city I walk through, usually with a coffee in hand.

members.name: Grace Fanson
members.bio: Hi! I’m Grace (she/her). I'm a PhD candidate in Planetary Sciences at MIT. I study planetary surface evolution on Mars and Earth. My research integrates numerical modeling, remote sensing data analysis, and geomorphology to deepen our understanding of the water cycle on early Mars. I am also involved with various mentorship projects in the department with the goal of making EAPS an even more connected and supportive environment. Outside of the Green Building, I enjoy pottery, reading, cycling, and cooking.

members.name: Ze-Wen Koh
members.bio: Hi there! I’m Ze-Wen (she/her), a PhD student in Planetary Science. I’m interested in the formation and evolution of planetary landscapes, and how they relate to global climate mechanisms and habitability. Currently, my research focuses primarily on rivers and lakes on Earth, Mars and Titan, and how they reflect past or present hydrological cycles. Before this, I obtained a B.A. in Physics and Computer Science at Cornell University. I grew up in Malaysia, and I love spending my time cooking dishes from home, playing board games, and watercolor painting!

members.name: Shaalin Sehra
members.bio: I’m Shaalin (she/her), a second-year PhD student in Planetary Science. I explore water-driven surface processes on Mars and their analogs on Earth, using remote sensing and computer modeling, coupled with fieldwork/labwork. Currently, I am using remote sensing to analyze landslide deposits in the Valles Marineris of Mars and doing fieldwork and lab experiments to study stream geomorphology in Cape Verde, an analog for Mars. When I’m not studying rocks, I love to climb them and teach others to climb!

members.name: Jensen Lawrence
members.bio: I’m Jensen (he/him), a PhD student in MIT’s Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences. My scientific interests are summarized by two broad questions: how do planetary systems form and evolve, and how do the surfaces and climates of terrestrial planetary bodies change over time? To address the former question, I conduct research in Prof. Richard Teague’s Planet Formation Lab. To address the latter question, I work with the Gaia Lab, using remote sensing data and computational models to study Mars’s geomorphic history. Previously, I obtained a BSc in mathematical physics from the University of Waterloo. In my free time I love to explore nature and study other languages.

members.name: Noella Aldrich
members.bio: I’m Noella, a third year undergraduate at MIT majoring in Earth, Atmosphere, and Planetary Science with a minor in Political Science. I’m working with Grace to study volcanic island river valleys on Earth to better understand how precipitation rates impact valley incision depth, and apply this to Martian river valleys. In my free time, I like to explore Boston with my friends and work on various craft projects.

members.name: Jack Gao
members.bio: Hi! I’m Jack (he/him), a senior in high school interested in geomorphology. I currently work on analyzing how stream networks behave in different climates as they develop over time. The goal is to better understand how streams impact their landscape and apply this understanding to other planetary bodies. In my free time I like to run, take photos, and play card games.

mascots.name: Io
mascots.bio: I don't know a lot about geomorphology or planetary science (despite my name), but I do enjoy sleeping, treats, chasing squirrels, and eating sticks. I can usually be found in my dad's or my mom's office in the Green Building, if you ever want to stop by and discuss some ideas (= give me some attention).

mascots.name: Catfish
mascots.bio: Meow, I’m Catfish! I’m a bit of a black sheep, or really black cat, and like to study plants instead of rocks and planetary surfaces. My methods include inspecting them with my paws and chewing on them to determine their taste and texture. When I’m not hard at work, you’ll find me playing, zooming, or stealing Io’s dog bed. I tend to be in the office Wednesdays and Fridays if you wanna say hi and play with me!
